memo.thesis_en: We own three shares, bought two days ago at $251.85, and the stock is down about 7.4% since. A two-day price move tells me nothing about the business, and I don't sell a good business because Mr. Market is in a mood. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of about 26.9%, debt-to-equity of 0.32, and owner earnings of roughly $9.26 billion against a $140 billion market cap. Its DCF says $437.57 a share against a price of $233.26, but that rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, so I treat the margin of safety as generous rather than gospel. What keeps me from adding with conviction is that the snapshot has no ten-year earnings record, no CEO tenure and no moat metrics, and the durability of a switching-cost moat in a fast-changing field is the question I must keep asking. I keep the position, size it modestly, and let the facts come in.

memo.management_assessment: Not assessable from this snapshot: CEO tenure, succession, insider ownership, compensation and capital allocation history are not reported. I cannot confirm criterion #4, so I give management no credit beyond what the returns on equity suggest.
memo.moat_analysis: My read is a switching-cost and client-relationship moat in technology and consulting services. The snapshot supports it only indirectly, through a 5-year average ROE of about 26.9%. Retention rates, pricing power and market share are not provided, so the moat is unverified. IT services is changing quickly, and a moat that must be continuously rebuilt is no moat, so I hold durability at roughly 10 years with low-to-moderate confidence.
memo.two_paragraph_business_description:
Accenture sells professional services to large corporations and governments: consulting, technology implementation, systems integration and outsourced operations. Clients hire its people to redesign processes, build and run software systems, and manage functions they would rather not run themselves.

It makes money by billing for the time and expertise of a large workforce, plus multi-year contracts to operate client systems. Because the business is people rather than factories, it needs little capital relative to earnings, which is consistent with the high ROE in the snapshot. The risks are pricing pressure, client budget cuts and technology shifts that reduce the labor needed.

memo.thesis_en: I don't own this one, and I'm going to pass. The numbers on the page are attractive: a 5-year average ROE of 22.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.43, and a price of $42.40 against a computed value of $75.94. But the snapshot gives me no description of the business, no earnings history, and no management record. Without those I can't say with confidence how it makes money or whether its moat will last ten years. A stock that looks cheap on a spreadsheet, in a field where the competitive ground may be shifting under it, is how I've lost money before. A 44% discount is no comfort if I can't tell whether the earnings power will be there in 2036. I'd rather miss this pitch than swing at one I can't see clearly. Invert: what could go wrong? Technology could erode the franchise, and I can't rule that out from here.

memo.thesis_en: I can explain how Best Buy makes money: it buys consumer electronics and appliances from a few big suppliers and resells them at thin margins. But I cannot find a moat I would bet ten years on. The same products can be bought online from rivals, and the suppliers can sell direct. The numbers in front of me look decent, with a 5-year average ROE of 48.4% and debt-to-equity of 0.37. But a ROE that high on a retailer may reflect a shrunken equity base as much as franchise strength, and the snapshot gives me nothing to check that. The 15.6% margin of safety only just clears my bar, and it rests on zero growth and a 5% discount rate, so a slight change in assumptions erases it. I would rather wait for a business with pricing power than pay a fair price for a hard-fought retail margin, so I pass.

The shares are down 16.04% from my entry at 128.38, but price decline alone is never a reason to sell. The record in front of me is a 5-year average ROE of 34.6% with debt-to-equity reported at 0.0, which is what a franchise with pricing power looks like. The model's intrinsic value of about $363 per share rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on it. Even a much more conservative number leaves room, so I keep what I own. My real worry is whether an apparel brand is a durable moat or a fashion cycle, and nothing in this snapshot settles that. I will not add until I can verify the earnings history and the brand's pricing power.

memo.thesis_en: I don't own Adobe, and this is a buy-or-wait question. I understand the business: creative and document software that people pay for by subscription, and that professionals have built their workflows around. On the snapshot, the numbers are attractive. The market cap is about $90.0 billion, five-year average ROE is 40.0%, debt-to-equity is 0.41, and the model's intrinsic value of $467.50 sits well above the $231.22 price. But a 5% discount rate and 8% growth produce a flattering number, and the snapshot doesn't let me test the thing that matters most, which is whether this moat survives a decade of rapid change in AI-generated content. It also doesn't show ten years of earnings, CEO tenure, or customer retention. Add a book that already holds ten names, and I'd rather wait than buy a cheap-looking price on faith. If the missing evidence confirms pricing power and retention, I'd want to own this.

Adobe sells software that creative professionals, marketers and office workers use to design, edit, and share content and documents. The best-known products are its creative suite and its PDF tools, mostly sold on subscription. A subscriber base that has built its workflows around the tools produces recurring revenue.

The company also sells digital experience software that helps businesses manage marketing, analytics and customer interactions. It makes money mainly from recurring subscription fees, with little capital needed to grow, which is why returns on equity are high. The key question is whether its tools stay indispensable as AI changes how content is made.

memo.thesis_en: I own General Dynamics, and the question is whether to keep it. The snapshot gives a 5-year average ROE of 17.2% and a debt-to-equity of 0.32, both inside my thresholds, and a margin of safety of 16.4%, just over my 15% bar, on an owner-earnings DCF with growth capped at 8% and a 5% discount rate. The moat is regulatory and intangible: submarines and other defense platforms where the government has few alternative suppliers and qualification barriers are high. It is not a Coca-Cola, and I cannot see in this snapshot the margin or backlog detail that would tell me how much pricing power exists. I paid $353.20 and the shares are down 1.2% after 21 days, which is noise to me, so I keep the position. I would not add aggressively on this evidence alone, because the margin of safety is thin and several of my checks could not be performed from these data.
